changes.title: A sent chat question keeps the things it was about as chips in its bubble, and a follow-up tells the model what earlier questions pointed at.

how.words: Builds the model's messages in one place, and now re-derives what each earlier turn pointed at from its stored refs, so a follow-up carries the pointed-at facts of the questions before it.

The end-to-end test now checks that a sent question shows its three refs as chips in its own bubble, that each chip opens its thing and survives a reload, that only the selection's chip stays above the box, and that a follow-up's prompt still lists what the earlier question pointed at.
`Turn` gains a `context` field holding the refs the question pointed at, sent back to the model with later questions and left out when empty.
A sent question is shown with chips in its bubble, each opening the part, data page, term or picture line it named, and the chips are kept with the stored conversation so they survive a reload.
The context box tracks the question's refs in the page state, so on sending the chips leave the box above while the selected part's chip stays.
Clicking a line chip in a sent question selects the matching line in the picture.
The clarify-with-AI end-to-end suite checks that a question gets a reply kept across a reload and that a follow-up is sent with the earlier turns, expecting the reply to report one turn so far.

changes.why: Before, the things a question was about vanished once it was sent, and the model only saw what the current question pointed at, so follow-ups like 'which of them comes first' lost their antecedents. Keeping the refs in the bubble and in the history makes multi-turn questions about selected parts, lines and data actually work.

off.code: `docair-ai.ask.messages` recomputes each earlier turn's pointed-at text from the current graph via `docair-ai.ask_context.about`; if the graph was re-scanned since that turn, the history describes the parts with today's facts, not what the model saw then.

changes.check: Check on the viewer side (not in these pieces) that the stored conversation actually round-trips the new field for old conversations without it.

changes.title: The AI now sees what kind of code item each part is, and its answers may not give data-flow tags to types.

how.words: A new list of symbol first-words that count as a code item, so `struct Cli` or `fn main` is recognised and a prose symbol is not.

New helper returning a part's code item; the digest now adds an `item` field for each node that has one, and reply checking uses it to strip `@in`/`@out`/`@calls` tags from changes to types and ask the model to retry without them.
The list of item kinds that are pure data, used to decide which parts must not send or take anything.

changes.why: Types are carried by the lines between parts; telling the model they send and take data produced wrong graph edits. Naming the item kind in the digest and rejecting data-flow tags on data items at reply-checking time, with one repair round, keeps the graph's data flows honest.
changes.check: Check that the tag-stripping partition also covers tags with different spacing or casing, and that a data-item change left with nothing after stripping is dropped deliberately.

changes.title: While a review runs, each request's answer is bound as soon as it arrives, so changes appear in order and the page can show each one as it is made.

how.words: `bind_answer` binds one request's reply into the run as soon as it returns (a failed or unreadable one leaves its pieces), and `explain_with` calls it per request in order instead of collecting all answers and binding at the end, while `bind` now resolves pieces against only that request's own batch.
A new run state holds the findings bound so far and answers that must wait for earlier requests, so each answer is bound in the requests' order the moment its predecessors are in.
The progress report now carries the changes bound so far, so they can go out with each progress update.
A running explain job is rendered as HTML: a bar of the requests answered with the job's words, then each change made so far with its title, piece count, findings and why.
The explain command prints each change's title to stderr as soon as it is bound, alongside the count of answered requests.
The end-to-end test for a served review now exercises the job flow, checking that a served page's review runs as a job and ends with its findings.

changes.why: So a served review can stream its findings: the changes so far go out with the progress and the reader sees each change as it is made, and binding in request order keeps the result the same as binding everything at the end.
changes.check: Check that a request whose answer arrives late cannot bind pieces an earlier request already took, since `taken` is shared but requests run concurrently.

changes.title: The review's wording names parts instead of piece ids.

how.words: `as_parts` rewrites each backtick-quoted piece id in the model's words to the part it stands for: a piece holding exactly one part becomes that part's id, and a prefixed id becomes the part's id when such a part exists.

changes.check: Check the case where a piece holds several parts: the id is then left as-is, which may still show internal ids to the reader.

changes.title: The documentation server no longer delays a rewrite while ignored files keep changing.

how.words: The quiet wait now restarts only for events that count (files that can change the documentation); events from ignored paths are consumed without restarting it, so a build writing an ignored folder no longer pushes the rewrite off forever.

changes.why: Before, any event at all restarted the quiet timer, so a busy build directory could starve the watcher and the documentation was never written again; now only relevant events delay it.
changes.check: Check that an ignored path really is classified as not counting for every kind of build output, since the fix depends entirely on that filter.

changes.title: When a review is asked in several parts, each request is told which pieces the other requests hold so it leaves them alone.

how.words: A new helper formats the list of pieces asked about elsewhere, telling the model never to put them into its changes, and the request packing reserves room for that list when there is more than one batch.

changes.why: Parallel requests each seeing only their own pieces would invent overlapping changes; naming the others' pieces keeps each change in one request, with the last request merging anything that spans parts.

off.code: The room reserved for the others' piece ids is subtracted once from the size limit; if the reduced limit still yields several batches, the added list of ids can push a request past the intended size.

changes.check: Check that a change genuinely spanning two parts is reliably left to the last request's merge and not duplicated by either part.

changes.title: In a chat conversation only one edit waits per part: a new edit of a part with one waiting is merged into it.

how.words: A new merge adds each reply's edit to the waiting ones, folding an edit of an already-waiting part into it: the newer summary and why win, tags add and remove cancel out, and whole-file or section edits replace the waiting one; it returns the parts whose waiting edit was replaced.
After a turn the command line prints, for each replaced part, that this reply's edit holds both the waiting one and the new one.
When taking a reply into the session, the answer reports which parts had an edit already waiting, and the chat HTML gains a note that the new edit replaced the waiting one.

changes.why: Successive replies editing the same part used to stack up conflicting edits; merging them keeps one coherent edit per part so applying the pending work does the last thing asked, and the user is told which edits were folded together.

off.code: When a tag edit is merged into a waiting edit, the waiting edit's mode, file and line are overwritten with the new edit's, so the merged edit may land on a different line or file than the one the user first asked about.

changes.check: Check that merging a removal of a tag the waiting edit added, and vice versa, leaves the pending edit in the state the user's latest words mean.

changes.title: A review older than the current changes says so, drops changes about pieces that are gone, and makes uncovered pieces changes of their own.

how.words: The review keeps only stored changes that still cover at least one existing piece, turns pieces the AI left out, the run did not reach, and pieces newer than the review into changes of their own in docair's words, explains in each case why it is docair's wording, and gives the review button a placeholder for live progress.
A new helper that pulls the piece-id lists a stored review keeps aside (`other`, `left`) out of the stored findings, so the stale-review checks can read them.

The review view now keeps only stored changes that still name at least one piece of the current change, adds the review's left-out pieces, the pieces the run did not reach, and the pieces newer than the review each as a change in docair's own words, and reports how many changes the review lists.
The changes page no longer counts stored review entries itself; it takes the count from the review view, so a stored change whose pieces are all gone no longer counts toward the Δ Changes button.

changes.why: A stored review otherwise shows changes about pieces that no longer exist and says nothing about new ones. Marking the docair-worded entries and offering to review again tells the reader the review is stale and how far it misses the current change.

off.code: A stored change none of whose pieces exist any more is dropped from the list entirely, together with what the AI found off in it; the page only says how many pieces the review misses, not which findings were thrown away.

changes.check: Check a stored change with some pieces still present: it should show only the surviving pieces and the missed-piece count should match.

changes.title: The AI proposes file edits only when the message asks for one.

how.words: The CLI end-to-end suite checks that a first question records only a walkthrough, while a follow-up that reports a missing edge produces an edit proposal in the patch, which docair apply writes into the code and the graph.

changes.why: A question that only asks for an explanation should not rewrite the project's files; an edit comes back only when the message itself asks for a correction, which the visible tests exercise from both sides.
changes.check: The changed test code below the cut, to confirm the suite now also covers the case where a message without a correction request brings no edit.
